blocks.content: 1. What Is an Anti-Pattern

Every codebase accumulates habits. Some of those habits solve a problem cleanly and become patterns worth reusing. Others solve the immediate problem while quietly making the next ten problems harder.

That second kind is an anti-pattern. It is not bad code by accident, it is a common, well intentioned response to a recurring situation that looks reasonable in the moment but turns out to be counterproductive once the codebase grows.
An anti-pattern is a common response to a recurring problem that appears reasonable at first but is ultimately counterproductive.

Anti-patterns are useful to learn precisely because they look like good decisions. A single class that "just handles orders" feels tidy on day one. A quick copy of a function feels faster than extracting a shared one. The trouble shows up later, when the shortcut has been repeated fifty times.

This lesson walks through five anti-patterns you will meet in almost every real project: the God Object, Spaghetti Code, the Golden Hammer, Copy Paste Programming, and Magic Numbers and Strings. For each one we look at what it looks like, why teams fall into it, and a concrete refactor that pulls the code back toward something maintainable.

["God Object, one class or module that knows and does too much","Spaghetti Code, control flow so tangled that no one can trace it confidently","Golden Hammer, forcing a single familiar tool onto every problem","Copy Paste Programming, duplicating code instead of extracting shared logic","Magic Numbers and Strings, unexplained literal values scattered through the code"]
items: God Object, one class or module that knows and does too much
Spaghetti Code, control flow so tangled that no one can trace it confidently
Golden Hammer, forcing a single familiar tool onto every problem
Copy Paste Programming, duplicating code instead of extracting shared logic
Magic Numbers and Strings, unexplained literal values scattered through the code

blocks.title: Why bother naming these
blocks.content: Naming an anti-pattern gives a team a shared vocabulary. Instead of a vague code review comment, you can say "this is turning into a God Object" and everyone knows roughly what is wrong and what to do about it.
2. God Object

A God Object is a single class or module that has grown to know about, and do, far more than its name suggests. It ends up touching the database, sending emails, calculating prices, and logging everything, all in one place.
What It Looks Like
The telltale sign is a class whose name is generic, like Manager, Handler, or Controller, and whose method list scrolls past several screens.
Below, an OrderManager class owns persistence, notifications, payments, and inventory. Any change to how email is sent means editing the same file that also calculates totals.

codes.python:
class OrderManager:
    def __init__(self, db, mailer, payment_gateway, inventory):
        self.db = db
        self.mailer = mailer
        self.payment_gateway = payment_gateway
        self.inventory = inventory

    def place_order(self, order):
        self.db.save("orders", order)
        self.inventory.reduce(order.items)
        self.payment_gateway.charge(order.customer_id, order.total)
        self.mailer.send(order.customer_email, "Order confirmed", order.summary())
        print("order placed:", order.id)

    def cancel_order(self, order_id):
        order = self.db.find("orders", order_id)
        self.inventory.restore(order.items)
        self.payment_gateway.refund(order.customer_id, order.total)
        self.mailer.send(order.customer_email, "Order cancelled", "Your order was cancelled.")
        print("order cancelled:", order_id)

blocks.content: Why It Happens
God Objects rarely start big. A class begins with one job, and every new feature request gets added to the class that already exists rather than a new one.
It feels efficient in the short term. There is no need to design a new abstraction, wire it up, or decide where it belongs. The cost is deferred until the class becomes too tangled to change safely.
How to Refactor Away From It
blocks.text: How to Refactor Away From It

blocks.content: The fix is to split responsibilities along the lines of what actually changes together. Persistence, notification, payment, and inventory each become their own focused class, and the original object becomes a thin coordinator.

Each class now has one reason to change. The payment logic can be tested and modified without touching notification code, and a new team member can understand OrderRepository in isolation instead of reading the whole system at once.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783494266236-505555894.png
blocks.alt: A single God Object connected to six unrelated responsibilities, compared with a coordinator delegating to several focused classes

blocks.title: A quick smell test
blocks.text: If you cannot describe a class in one short sentence without using the word "and", it is probably drifting toward a God Object.

blocks.content: 3. Spaghetti Code

Spaghetti Code describes control flow that has no clear structure. Conditions nest inside loops inside conditions, functions jump into each other unpredictably, and state changes happen in places far from where they are read.
What It Looks Like
The classic shape is a long function with deeply nested if statements, shared mutable flags, and logic for several unrelated concerns interleaved line by line.
Why It Happens

Spaghetti Code usually grows one small addition at a time. Each new rule gets bolted onto the existing function because that is where the related logic already lives, and nobody wants to be the one who stops to restructure it.
Under deadline pressure, adding one more if statement always looks cheaper than pulling the function apart. Repeated many times, that cheap choice compounds into something nobody wants to touch.
How to Refactor Away From It
blocks.text: How to Refactor Away From It

blocks.content: The remedy is to separate concerns into small, named functions, each doing one job, and to replace nested conditionals with early returns or lookup tables.

Each function now answers one question and can be tested on its own. The top level processCheckout reads almost like a sentence describing the business rule, instead of a maze you have to step through mentally.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499336728-130888744.png
blocks.alt: Comparison of tangled nested conditional flow against a clean sequence of small named functions for checkout logic

blocks.title: A useful heuristic
blocks.content: If you cannot point to where a piece of logic lives without scrolling through a large function, that is a sign the function is doing the job of several smaller ones.
4. Golden Hammer

The Golden Hammer anti-pattern is naming a favorite tool, pattern, or technology and then reaching for it on every problem, whether it fits or not. The phrase comes from the old line that if all you have is a hammer, everything looks like a nail.
What It Looks Like

A team that loves the Observer pattern might wire up event listeners for things that are really just a direct function call. A team that loves inheritance might build a five level class hierarchy to express what a single conditional would have handled.
Below, a simple discount calculation is forced through an elaborate Strategy and Factory setup even though there are only two discount types and they never change independently.
Why It Happens
Familiarity is comfortable. A pattern that worked well on a previous project builds confidence, and reaching for it again feels safe even when the new problem has different shape.
It is also reinforced by habit, not malice. A developer who just learned about the Strategy pattern is naturally eager to apply it, and the codebase ends up with more ceremony than the problem needs.
How to Refactor Away From It
blocks.text: How to Refactor Away From It

blocks.content: The fix is to match the tool to the actual shape of the problem. Two fixed discount tiers that never change independently do not need a Strategy hierarchy or a Factory, a plain lookup does the same job with less code to read.

If a sixth discount tier appears with genuinely different behavior, for example one that depends on time of day and another that depends on order history, that is when a Strategy interface earns its keep. Reach for the pattern when the variation demands it, not by default.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499338398-874555920.png
blocks.alt: The same favorite pattern forced onto three unrelated problems versus matching a plain lookup table to the actual need

blocks.title: A question worth asking
blocks.text: Before reaching for your favorite pattern, ask what would happen if you solved this with the simplest possible code first, and only add structure when a second real requirement shows up.

blocks.content: 5. Copy Paste Programming

Copy Paste Programming is duplicating a block of code to reuse its behavior instead of extracting it into a shared function. It is quick in the moment, and it quietly multiplies the cost of every future bug fix.
What It Looks Like
Two functions validating a signup form and a profile update form look nearly identical, because one was copied from the other and tweaked slightly.
When the email validation rule needs to change, someone has to remember to update it in both places. In a codebase with ten copies instead of two, that memory always fails eventually.
Why It Happens

Copying an existing function is the fastest way to get something working right now, especially under deadline pressure. Extracting a shared helper takes a few extra minutes of thought about naming and parameters.
It is also encouraged by unclear ownership. If nobody is responsible for the shape of the validation layer as a whole, each new form just gets its own copy rather than reusing what exists.
How to Refactor Away From It
blocks.text: How to Refactor Away From It

blocks.content: Extract the shared rules into small, named validator functions, and compose them per form. Each rule is written once and tested once.
Now the email rule exists in one place. Fixing it once fixes it everywhere it is used, and adding a new form is just a matter of listing which rules apply.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499340102-914772401.png
blocks.alt: Two validation functions each duplicating the same email rule versus both calling one shared rules object

blocks.title: Rule of thumb
blocks.content: The first duplication is often fine to leave alone. The moment you are about to paste a third copy of the same logic, that is the signal to extract a shared function.
6. Magic Numbers and Strings

Magic numbers and magic strings are unexplained literal values sitting directly in the middle of logic. The number 0.07 might be a tax rate, a discount, or a rounding threshold, and the code gives no clue which.
What It Looks Like
Literals like 3, 86400, and "PENDING" are scattered through the code with no name attached, so their meaning has to be guessed from context or from asking whoever wrote them.

A reader has to reverse engineer that 86400 is seconds in a day, that 1.0725 is a tax multiplier for California, and that "PENDING" is one of some fixed set of statuses that exists nowhere as a single list.
Why It Happens

Typing a literal value is the path of least resistance while you are focused on getting a calculation right. Naming it as a constant feels like a side task that can happen later, and later often does not come.

String literals for statuses are especially easy to let slip in, since there is no compiler error for typing "Pending" in one place and "PENDING" in another, the mismatch just silently fails at runtime.
How to Refactor Away From It
blocks.text: How to Refactor Away From It

blocks.content: Give every meaningful literal a name. Group related constants together, use an enum-like structure for fixed sets of strings, and let the code read close to the business rule it represents.

The logic functions are now short and readable, and every rate or duration lives in one clearly named place. Changing the New York tax rate means editing one line, not searching the codebase for 1.08875.
https://algorithmxlr8-assets-images.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/lld-images/1783499343194-378975431.png
blocks.alt: Scattered unnamed literals feeding two functions versus a single named constants module supplying both

7. Weighing the Tradeoffs of Fixing Anti-Patterns
blocks.text: 7. Weighing the Tradeoffs of Fixing Anti-Patterns

blocks.content: Refactoring away from an anti-pattern is not free. It takes time, it touches working code, and it can introduce new bugs if done carelessly. It helps to be honest about both sides before starting a cleanup.

{"pros":["Smaller, focused units are easier to test and reason about","Shared logic lives in one place, so fixes and rule changes apply everywhere at once","New team members ramp up faster when code maps clearly to the concepts it represents","Bugs become easier to isolate because responsibilities are separated"],"cons":["Refactoring takes real time away from shipping new features","Over-correcting can add unnecessary abstraction where simple code would have been fine","Extracting shared code too early can create the wrong abstraction that is hard to undo","Large refactors carry a risk of regressions if not covered by tests"]}

That last row on the pros side matters more than it looks. The goal of fixing an anti-pattern is never structure for its own sake, it is making the next change cheaper and safer than it would have been.
8. Recognizing Anti-Patterns Early
Every anti-pattern in this lesson starts from a reasonable decision made under real constraints. Nobody sets out to build a God Object, it accumulates one convenient addition at a time.
That is why catching them early matters more than fixing them late. A class with six responsibilities is a quick split today, and a genuinely painful untangling in a year.
Signals Worth Watching For

["A class name that needs the word \"and\" to describe what it does","A function whose behavior you cannot summarize in one sentence","The same block of logic appearing in more than one file","A pattern applied because it was used last time, not because this problem needs it","A literal value whose meaning requires asking someone else or reading old commits"]
items: A class name that needs the word "and" to describe what it does
A function whose behavior you cannot summarize in one sentence
The same block of logic appearing in more than one file
A pattern applied because it was used last time, not because this problem needs it
A literal value whose meaning requires asking someone else or reading old commits

blocks.content: A Practical Habit

Code review is the natural place to catch these. When a diff adds a fourth responsibility to an existing class, pastes a block that already exists elsewhere, or drops in an unexplained number, that is worth a comment before it merges.

blocks.title: None of this is about perfection
blocks.content: A small amount of duplication or a slightly oversized class is not an emergency. The goal is to notice the pattern before it compounds across the whole codebase, not to chase an idealized structure from day one.
9. Bringing It Together

God Objects, Spaghetti Code, the Golden Hammer, Copy Paste Programming, and Magic Numbers all share the same origin story. Each one is a shortcut that solved today's problem while making tomorrow's problem larger.

The refactors are not complicated on their own. Split responsibilities, flatten control flow into small named functions, choose tools that match the actual problem, extract shared logic, and name your constants.

What is hard is noticing the anti-pattern while it is still small, before the class has forty methods or the literal 0.07 has been copied into twelve files. That noticing is a habit worth building, and it pays for itself the first time a bug fix takes one line instead of ten.
Clean code is rarely written that way from the first draft, it gets there by someone noticing the anti-pattern and refactoring before it spreads.

Keep this lesson as a checklist during code review. If a change smells like one of these five patterns, it is far cheaper to name it and adjust course now than to untangle it after it has spread through the rest of the system.
